 Show biography 
 Rob White specialises in pensions, tax and savings. He writes in-depth analyses of public sector pension schemes, including how Royal Mail still costs taxpayers £3.8m a day . He previously worked at StepChange Debt Charity, the Money and Pensions Service, and as a local journalist in New Zealand. He can be reached at  rob.white@telegraph.co.uk  and @robwhitepress 
 Published 
 31 October 2026 7:30am GMT
 Thousands of grieving families will no longer be charged income tax when inherited pensions arrive late, the Government has confirmed.
 Defined contribution pots are passed on tax-free when the saver dies before age 75, but beneficiaries are currently charged at their marginal rate on payments that are delayed for more than two years.
 However, this time limit was removed from Oct 28 under new rules outlined in the Budget.
 The change means recipients will save up to £45,000 on a £100,000 payout.
 Income tax will still be charged when pension savers die after age 75, and the changes do not affect inheritance tax.
 Experts believe the move will save thousands of people from falling into an “unnecessary tax trap” because of administrative delays or estate disputes.
 Pension savers can choose who receives their unspent pots when they die using an expression of wish form, even if they hadn’t reached retirement age. The forms are not legally binding, but are considered by pension providers when deciding who inherits the funds.
 If someone dies under the age of 75, income tax is not levied unless the payout took more than two years from when the scheme was first notified of the death.
 The Government estimated that abolishing this charge would save beneficiaries around £15m a year.

 Rob Morgan, of Charles Stanley, said: “This removes an unnecessary tax trap from the pensions system. Beneficiaries should not be penalised because administrative delays or estate disputes prolong a payment beyond an arbitrary deadline.
 “With pension administrators set to take on significant new inheritance tax responsibilities next year, the potential for delays is likely to increase. Removing this cliff-edge rule is a timely and pragmatic reform that brings greater certainty for families at a difficult time.”
 Delays of more than two years are rare, but they can happen with complex pension schemes or where no expression of wish form was drawn up. Beneficiaries can also be hard to trace if they have ignored letters, moved abroad or lost touch with the deceased and were not expecting an inheritance.
 From April 2027, pensions will also be assessed for inheritance tax, which will generate a combined tax rate of up to 67pc on large pots if income tax is also charged.
 Clare Moffat, of pensions provider Royal London, said: “Sorting out pension death benefits can take time. That might be because beneficiaries are difficult to find, there are complex family circumstances and no expression of wish from the person who died, or because potential beneficiaries have died or are unwell.
 “This is a welcome change for thousands of beneficiaries. It means the income tax treatment is fair for all who inherit defined contribution pensions, where the person died under the age of 75, and the date someone receives their payment is no longer important tax-wise.”
 An HMRC spokesman said: “We’re removing the two-year deadline to ensure bereaved families aren’t unfairly affected by delays outside their control.”
